title: Orion Medical - On-prem Airgapped Discovery
summary: Discovery call to understand Orion Medical's requirements for an on-prem, air-gapped deployment of Redwood Private. Key concerns: offline update process, signed model/artifact delivery, hardware constraints (rack/power/GPU type), encryption/KMS integration, audit logging, and pilot scope. Agreed next steps include sharing security pack, proposed pilot design (2-node cluster), and scheduling an on-site workshop for hardware/network validation.
action_items: Emily Chen: Send security pack (SOC2, ISO certs, architecture diagrams) by 2025-09-17
Carlos Ramos: Draft pilot technical plan (2-node onprem cluster, benchmark plan) by 2025-09-19
Marcus Lee: Share current hardware inventory and rack specs by 2025-09-18
Aisha Khan: Provide list of required compliance artifacts and KMS vendor constraints by 2025-09-20
next_steps: Redwood to send security and deployment docs
Schedule 90-min on-site workshop for hardware/network validation
Agree pilot scope and success criteria (latency, throughput, cost targets)
Exchange signed NDA for deeper audit docs if needed
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2025-09-15 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Emily Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ramos (Redwood SE), Dr. Sana Patel (CTO, Orion), Marcus Lee (ML Infra Lead), Aisha Khan (Security Architect), Tom Reeves (Compliance Manager)

Summary: quick discovery focused on on-prem/air-gapped deployment constraints for regulated healthcare workloads; customer wants details on offline updates, hardware, and compliance.

00:00 Emily Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, really appreciate folks making time. I'm Emily from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. with me is Carlos, our solutions engineer. Just to kick off, can everyone do a quick intro?
00:14 Dr. Sana Patel: Sana here, CTO at Orion, we run clinical data pipelines and some LLM-powered triage tools, sensitive PHI so we need air-gapped.
00:21 Marcus Lee: Marcus, ML infra lead, I manage our GPU clusters and model deployment. We're evaluating options: hosted/dedicated/private and leaning heavily to private on-prem because of regulation.
00:29 Aisha Khan: Aisha, security architect, I'm focused on KMS, key custody, and how updates happen in an air-gapped environment.
00:34 Tom Reeves: Tom, compliance, looking for audit trails and documentation — SOC2 is table stakes, and we have internal ISO requirements too.
00:41 Carlos Ramos: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: understand your constraints, talk about Redwood Private options for on-prem/air-gapped, discuss update/signing workflow, hardware and network constraints, and outline a pilot.
00:50 Emily Chen: Perfect. Sana, could you describe the main blocker pushing you to on-prem?
00:56 Dr. Sana Patel: Sure, it's mostly PHI and a few contracts with hospitals that require no internet egress from our inference stack. We also have a procurement window and need to show how model updates are controlled — basically no auto pull from external registries.
01:12 Marcus Lee: We're also limited on racks and power in our colo. We currently have two 42U racks and depending on GPU type, we might need to rework power distribution. We prefer H100 but cost and lead times are a problem; A100s or 80GB A100 L4 are options.
01:27 Emily Chen: Understood. Carlos, do you want to describe how Redwood supports air-gapped deployments?
01:31 Carlos Ramos: Yeah. So in our typical Private on-prem workflow, there's a customer-managed control plane or optional Redwood control plane with restricted connectivity. For air-gapped, we provide signed model artifacts and container bundles that you can import via a secure jumpbox or removable media. Updates are delivered as signed tarballs that our installer validates against a public key that you control — or we can integrate with your HSM for validation keys.
01:56 Aisha Khan: Wait, signed bundles — how does key rotation work? We cannot have private keys sitting on the same offline hosts.
02:03 Carlos Ramos: Right, we recommend integrating with an HSM or BYOK in KMS — the typical pattern is signing occurs in your secure signing environment, we verify signatures at install-time using a public key, or we do mutual TLS from an import appliance. For key rotation you'd rotate signing keys in your signing environment and produce new signed artifacts. None of the signing private keys need to be on the inference hosts.
02:24 Tom Reeves: Are there examples of customers doing air-gapped updates via sftp to a bastion host? We're leaning to that model, but need to ensure chain-of-custody.
02:33 Carlos Ramos: Yes, sftp to a hardened jumpbox/bastion is common. Usually the jumpbox has restricted egress only to a validation API that's internal, or no egress at all — everything validated locally. We also support checksums, signed manifests, and attestation logs.
02:48 Marcus Lee: For drivers and CUDA, do you ship a full OS image or do we manage driver updates? We don't want automatic kernel updates.
02:55 Carlos Ramos: Drivers and NVIDIA stack are typically managed by you. Redwood provides container images built against supported CUDA versions; for air-gapped installs we hand over the images and a compatibility matrix. We can also provide a vendor-validated driver bundle for offline install if you need. Kernel upgrades stay under your control.
03:12 Dr. Sana Patel: What's the typical hardware footprint for a production node for Redwood inference? We want numbers to bring to procurement.
03:18 Carlos Ramos: For a small pilot, commonly a two-node setup with each node having 4 x A100 80GB (or 2-4 H100 if you're going for highest performance). If you're constrained, 2 x A100-per-node is workable for low throughput. You'll also need roughly 512GB-1TB RAM per node depending on concurrent sessions and a fast NVMe for KV cache. Networking: 100Gbps recommended for multi-GPU scaling.
03:41 Marcus Lee: Power per rack — any ballpark? Our colo charges are strict.
03:45 Carlos Ramos: Depends on GPU. H100s draw more power; ballpark is 20-30kW per rack fully loaded. A100s less but still substantial. We'll share a spec sheet.
03:55 Emily Chen: We'll include power and thermal numbers in the docs. On compliance: Tom, what audit artifacts are you expecting?
04:01 Tom Reeves: We need audit logs, access control logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC mapping, and evidence of encryption at rest and in transit. Also ability to show who pushed a model and when, preferably with signed audit events.
04:14 Carlos Ramos: Redwood Private provides audit logs at the route/token/model level. For air-gapped installs we store logs locally and can stream to your ELK/Splunk on-prem. We can also support signed audit events and tamper-evident storage if you supply a write-once storage or HSM-backed signing.
04:32 Aisha Khan: What about key management — does Redwood integrate with external HSMs like Thales or Azure Key Vault?
04:38 Carlos Ramos: Yes, we support KMIP-compatible HSMs and common KMS providers, also HSM appliances. For air-gapped, often customers use a local HSM. We can plug into your KMS for encrypting token material and disk encryption keys; master keys remain in your control.
04:51 Dr. Sana Patel: Model provenance is important. We need to ensure the model binary hasn't been tampered with between signing and install.
04:58 Carlos Ramos: That's the role of signed manifests + checksum verification + attestation. We can also provide deterministic SBOMs for the runtime images so you can verify what's inside.
05:10 Marcus Lee: Any restrictions on GPUs from Redwood side? Some inference runtimes need particular driver versions, and we have older generation hardware.
05:16 Carlos Ramos: We publish a compatibility matrix. Older gen GPUs may still work but with lower perf and might not support certain optimizations. For quantized float16 kernels, we target Ampere+ typically. We'll share exact minimal supported specs.
05:27 Aisha Khan: Patching cadence — we have blackout windows for clinical systems. How do we handle urgent security patches?
05:33 Emily Chen: Good question, we design the pilot to respect your maintenance windows. For critical patches, if it's a vulnerability in the runtime, we provide a signed hotfix artifact and coordinate a one-time emergency push via your jumpbox, with full rollback artifacts.
05:47 Tom Reeves: Licensing model — is this consumption or seat? We need to model costs for procurement.
05:52 Emily Chen: For Private on-prem we typically do a platform fee plus optional reserved capacity pricing for Dedicated. For strict on-prem air-gapped there's a yearly license plus support tiers. We'll send a draft commercial proposal with options.
06:05 Dr. Sana Patel: For the pilot, we want to validate latency and cost per inference for our triage model (seq length ~1024). Can Redwood run benchmarks offline?
06:13 Carlos Ramos: Yes, we can provide a benchmark harness and a dockerized offline runner that you can execute in your environment; results are reproducible. For air-gapped we'll hand over the harness and a signed model artifact and you run it locally, then upload results to the shared secure folder.
06:28 Marcus Lee: Good. Also, what's the rollback story if an update causes regressions?
06:32 Carlos Ramos: We keep previous signed artifacts and support atomic rollbacks. The install process creates a snapshot and you can roll back to prior image; we also recommend snapshotting volumes before upgrades.
06:40 Aisha Khan: Network topologies — we have a strict zero-egress policy. Can the installer run fully offline?
06:44 Carlos Ramos: Yes, installer can run fully offline. We provide a signed bundle and an installer binary that performs local validations. No egress required.
06:51 Emily Chen: Great. Quick question on stakeholders and timeline — Sana, what's your target for a pilot?
06:56 Dr. Sana Patel: We'd like to have a pilot in Q4, ideally late October, but procurement may push it. We have a board deadline early November to present vendor recommendations.
07:06 Emily Chen: Noted. Marcus, any procurement lead times for GPUs?
07:09 Marcus Lee: H100 lead times are months; A100s are faster. We'll confirm what's feasible and share inventory.
07:15 Carlos Ramos: For the pilot we can design for A100 or even mixed nodes; performance adjustments are clear.
07:20 Tom Reeves: On documentation, we'll need an NDA to receive full security docs.
07:24 Emily Chen: We'll send an NDA and the security pack. Carlos will include the installation checklist and pilot plan.
07:29 Dr. Sana Patel: One more thing — for data residency, all inference logs must remain in our VPC/colo.
07:35 Carlos Ramos: Understood; Redwood Private respects that and logs remain local unless you configure a stream to your aggregator.
07:40 Marcus Lee: Any partner solutions for procurement or hardware validation?
07:43 Emily Chen: We work with a few partners for validated racks and OEMs; we can introduce you if helpful.
07:50 Dr. Sana Patel: That would be useful.
07:53 Emily Chen: Ok wrapping up, quick recap and next steps?
07:56 Tom Reeves: Recap: security docs + NDA, pilot plan, hardware spec sheet, on-site workshop.
08:02 Emily Chen: Yep. Action items we captured — we'll send docs and schedule the workshop. Any final questions?
08:08 Aisha Khan: Just to confirm, signed artifacts + HSM integration covers our primary concerns.
08:13 Carlos Ramos: Correct. We'll include key rotation patterns and attestation examples in the pack.
08:18 Dr. Sana Patel: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the pilot plan.
08:21 Emily Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with timelines.

End of transcript.

References/links mentioned: security pack (link to be shared), pilot plan (Redwood draft), compatibility matrix (will be attached).

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some words may be mis-attributed, proper nouns occasionally off.
